verses.text: Jesus turned to his disciples.The Pharisees were still listening. "A rich man had a manager who ran his estate — contracts, debtors, all of it. Then someone accused the manager of squandering everything.

footnotes.content: The Greek word (διασκορπίζων) is the same root Luke used in 15:13 for the prodigal son "squandering" his inheritance. The verbal echo is deliberate: two men face crisis after waste, but their responses diverge radically. The prodigal grovels; the manager calculates.

verses.text: The rich man summoned him. 'What's this I hear? Hand over the books. You're finished.'

Alone now, the manager thought it through. What was he going to do? His position — gone. The only life he knew — over.He could dig ditches, but a man of his standing didn't do that kind of work. He could beg, but the shame of it would kill him before the hunger did.

footnotes.content: The manager's two rejected options — digging and begging — are not about physical ability. In the ancient honor-shame system, digging (σκάπτειν) was the work of slaves and the lowest-status laborers. For a professional estate manager to dig would be class annihilation — the permanent loss of everything that defined his social identity. Begging (ἐπαιτεῖν) was even worse: a public declaration that you had no patrons, no network, no one willing to support you. Both were forms of social death.

verses.text: Then something cleared. 'I know what I'll do. I'll make sure that when I lose this job, there are doors open for me.'
He moved quickly. He called in the master's debtors, one at a time.
'How much do you owe?' 'A hundred jugs of olive oil.' 'Take your contract. Sit down. Write fifty.'

footnotes.keyword: a hundred jugs of olive oil
footnotes.content: A hundred "baths" (βάτους) of olive oil = approximately 850 gallons, worth roughly 1,000 denarii — about three years' wages for a common laborer. This is not a household debt but a massive commercial transaction. The fifty percent reduction the manager arranges is a fortune in itself.

verses.text: The man wrote. The next debtor came in. 'How much?' 'A hundred sacks of wheat.' 'Write eighty.'

footnotes.content: A hundred "cors" (κόρους) of wheat = approximately 1,000 bushels, the harvest of roughly 100 acres. The twenty percent reduction (from 100 to 80) was smaller in proportion but still represented an enormous sum. By having each debtor rewrite his own contract (γράψον — "you write"), the manager ensures no forgery is attributable to him. The debtors' own handwriting makes the deals legally binding.

verses.text: Each one walked out owing less — and owing him. His master found out.And grudgingly, he had to admit it: the man had played it brilliantly. He commended his dishonest manager — not for the ethics, but for the foresight."The people of this world," Jesus observed, "are shrewder in dealing with their own kind than the people of the light."

footnotes.content: The "master" (ὁ κύριος) in v. 8a is the estate owner within the story — not Jesus. Jesus begins speaking in his own voice from v. 9 ("And I tell you..."). The commendation is grudgingly ironic: the master has been outmaneuvered. If he rescinds the debt reductions, he destroys the reputation for generosity the manager has just created in his name. The manager has used the patron-client system against the patron.

The Greek φρονίμως ("shrewdly") is morally neutral — it describes practical intelligence and foresight, not ethical approval. Jesus is not commending dishonesty. He is making an argument from lesser to greater (a minori ad maius): if a rogue plans ahead with this much intelligence to secure his earthly future, how much more should God's people plan for the eschatological future that is arriving?

"Children of this age" (υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου) versus "children of the light" (υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός) is a binary familiar from the Dead Sea Scrolls (the Community Rule, 1QS 3:13–4:26). In the Qumran framework, these terms identified eschatological allegiance — which cosmic side you had chosen. Jesus uses the categories but inverts the expected conclusion: the "children of this age" are actually better at long-range planning than the supposedly enlightened community.

verses.text: Then, to them all: "Use the wealth of this world to build friendships. When it's gone — and it will be gone — you'll be received into homes that last forever.

footnotes.content: The Greek "mammon of unrighteousness" (μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας) is an Aramaic loanword paired with a characterizing genitive: wealth that belongs to the domain of systemic unrighteousness. It is not merely "dishonestly obtained money" but wealth that operates within a fundamentally broken system. Jesus does not say to reject it — he says to use it strategically to build relationships that outlast the system itself.

"Eternal tents" (αἰωνίους σκηνάς) echoes the tabernacle/booth tradition — temporary structures that become permanent dwelling places in the age to come. The paradox is deliberate: "tents" are by definition impermanent, yet these are "eternal." Some scholars (Nolland) read this as the welcome of the grateful poor in the eschatological community; others (Wright) as the heavenly dwelling place itself.

verses.text: If you can't be trusted with what belongs to someone else, who would give you something of your own?

footnotes.content: These three parallel sayings apply the parable's logic to daily life. "Very little" (ἐλάχιστον) is not a dismissal of wealth but a recalibration: compared to "true riches" (τὸ ἀληθινόν), all earthly wealth is small change. The progression builds: faithful/dishonest (v. 10), worldly/true riches (v. 11), another's/your own (v. 12). Each contrast asks the same question differently: can you be trusted? The early church understood this as a test of character before responsibility, not a promise that faithfulness would be rewarded with more money.

verses.text: "No slave can serve two masters. You will hate the one and love the other. You will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and Mammon."

footnotes.content: In v. 13, Mammon (μαμωνᾷ) is personified — not merely "wealth" but a rival lord demanding the allegiance that belongs to God alone. The capitalization reflects the Greek: here the word functions as a proper noun with an implied definite article. The household slave (οἰκέτης) image makes the impossibility physical, not merely theoretical: ancient slaves belonged entirely to one master. Split loyalty was not a character flaw but a structural impossibility.

footnotes.keyword: You cannot serve both God and Mammon
footnotes.content: Is this really an either/or? Three frames: (1) The economic realist notes that wealth is a tool — the problem is not money but its misuse, and Jesus' binary is hyperbolic rhetoric designed to provoke. (2) The social psychologist observes that research on materialism (Kasser, Ryan) consistently shows that wealth-orientation correlates with decreased empathy, ethical flexibility, and relational satisfaction — the binary may be less hyperbolic than it appears. (3) The theological reader hears the claim that wealth is not neutral: it actively competes for the loyalty, attention, and identity that constitute "service" (δουλεύειν). The word is not "use" but "serve as a slave." Jesus is not asking whether you can own things while believing in God; he is asking which master determines your decisions when they conflict.

verses.text: The Pharisees heard all of it.They loved money — and what he was saying cut too close. They sneered at him.Not a quiet disagreement. Open contempt.

footnotes.content: Luke provides the motive for the Pharisees' contempt: they were φιλάργυροι ("money-lovers"). This is not an ad hominem attack but an explanation of why the preceding teaching about mammon provoked such hostility. Their financial self-interest made Jesus' money-or-God binary personally threatening. The imperfect tense of ἐξεμυκτήριζον ("they kept sneering") indicates sustained, physical contempt — the word literally means "to turn up the nose at."

verses.text: Jesus looked at them. "You spend your lives justifying yourselves in front of other people. But God knows your hearts. And what people prize most highly is what God finds detestable.

footnotes.content: The Greek βδέλυγμα ("abomination, detestable thing") is Septuagint language for covenant violation — the same word used for idolatry (Deut 7:25–26), for the "abomination of desolation" (Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11), and for practices that violate the fundamental relationship between God and Israel. Jesus is not merely saying God disapproves of human status-seeking. He is using the strongest possible covenant-violation language: what humans exalt is, in God's sight, idolatry.

verses.text: But do not misunderstand — heaven and earth will disappear before one stroke of a single letter of the Law does."

footnotes.keyword: the kingdom of God has been announced
footnotes.content: The phrase βιάζεται (middle voice: "is being pressed into" or "everyone is forcing their way in") has been debated since antiquity. Does it mean the kingdom "suffers violence" (passive) or "is being entered with urgency" (middle)? In context — following the announcement that the kingdom has been proclaimed since John — the positive sense is more likely: people are responding with eager urgency. The verse does NOT mean the Law is abolished; v. 17 immediately corrects that misreading.

footnotes.keyword: one stroke of a single letter
footnotes.content: The "stroke" (κεραία) refers to the tiny distinguishing marks on Hebrew letters — the serif or pen-stroke that differentiates, for example, a ד (dalet) from a ר (resh). Jesus' hyperbole is precise: not even the smallest distinguishing mark of the Torah will fall away. This saying prevents the supersessionist misreading that vv. 16 might suggest: the kingdom does not replace the Law but fulfills it.

verses.text: He went on: "Every man who sends his wife away and marries another woman commits adultery. And a man who marries a woman sent away by her husband commits adultery too."

footnotes.content: In first-century Jewish law, only the husband could initiate divorce (ἀπολύω, literally "release/send away"). Women had no legal standing to divorce their husbands. Jesus' saying is protective: by declaring the divorcing husband guilty of adultery (μοιχεύει), he removes the unilateral power men held over women's marital status and economic security. A divorced woman in the ancient world lost her home, her social standing, and often her means of survival. The saying illustrates the Law's enduring ethical force (v. 17): even in the new era of the kingdom, the Torah's protection of the vulnerable stands.

footnotes.keyword: Every man who sends his wife away
footnotes.content: This saying appears abruptly after the kingdom proclamation and Law affirmation of vv. 16–17. Why? Luke places it as a concrete example of the Law's continuing authority: the Torah's protection of women in marriage is not abolished by the kingdom's arrival. The divorce saying also appears in Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 (with an exception clause) and Mark 10:11–12. Paul discusses the topic in 1 Corinthians 7:10–16. The canonical voices together address a range of pastoral situations; Luke's version is the most absolute, emphasizing the prophetic protection of the vulnerable party.

verses.text: "There was a rich man. He dressed in purple and fine linen— fabrics that cost more than most people earned in a year — and he feasted lavishly.Not occasionally. Every single day.

footnotes.content: Purple dye was extracted from murex mollusks — tiny sea snails harvested off the coasts of Tyre and Sidon. Pliny the Elder (Natural History 9.62) reports that Tyrian purple cost more per weight than gold in some market periods. Fine linen (βύσσος) was imported from Egypt, where it was produced using labor-intensive methods. Together, these two fabrics identify someone at the apex of conspicuous wealth — roughly equivalent to a modern billionaire's display of private jets and couture. The iterative imperfect (ἐνεδιδύσκετο, "was accustomed to wearing") establishes this as daily lifestyle, not occasional luxury.

The rich man is deliberately unnamed — a stunning reversal of ancient naming conventions. In antiquity, being named meant being socially visible; anonymity was social death. In this parable, the beggar gets a name and the rich man doesn't. Post-2010 scholarship (Van Eck, Levine/Witherington) reads this as a narrative enactment of the eschatological reversal: the person who matters to God has a name; the person who mattered to the world is rendered anonymous in the only account that will last. The later tradition supplied the name "Dives" (Latin for "rich"), but Luke's refusal to name him is the point.

verses.text: He longed for scraps— even the bread the rich man's guests used to wipe their hands and tossed under the table. Street dogs came and licked his open wounds.Not pets. Scavengers. They treated a living man the way they would treat a corpse.

footnotes.content: Lazarus (Λάζαρος, from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר, Eleazar = "God has helped") is the only named character in any of Jesus' parables. The name is the parable's theological time-bomb: the person whose name means "God has helped" is the person no human helps. Jerome observed: "The meaning of Lazarus's name is one who has been helped — not a helper, but one who has been helped." The divine promise is embedded in the character's identity before the story delivers on it.

The πυλών ("gateway, vestibule") is the grand entrance of a wealthy estate — the semi-public threshold between the rich man's world and the public street. Lazarus was unavoidable. The rich man passed him every single day (the imperfect tenses of v. 19 establish habitual daily practice). The perfect passive ἐβέβλητο ("had been laid/thrown") indicates Lazarus was placed there by others — he lacked the physical strength to get there himself.

footnotes.keyword: Street dogs came and licked his open wounds
footnotes.content: Dogs (κύνες) in first-century Palestine were not household pets but street scavengers — ritually unclean animals associated with corpse-licking (1 Kings 22:38; 2 Kings 9:36). That dogs are licking Lazarus's sores (ἕλκη) means they are treating him as already a corpse. Keener notes that dogs' saliva would have stung open wounds rather than soothed them. This is not comfort — it is maximum social degradation: a human being, alive but treated as a carcass, receiving physical contact only from unclean scavengers.

verses.text: Then Lazarus died.No one buried him. But angels carried him to Abraham's side. The rich man died too. He was buried.

footnotes.content: "Abraham's bosom" (κόλπος Ἀβραάμ) is not spatial anatomy but banquet imagery. At formal meals, guests reclined on couches; the position nearest the host — reclining against the host's chest — was the supreme seat of honor. John uses the identical image for the Beloved Disciple at the Last Supper (John 13:23 — ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ). Lazarus is now in the place of highest honor at the eschatological feast, with Abraham as host of God's people. The reversal is complete: the man who longed for scraps from the rich man's table now reclines at the head of Abraham's table.

The parable mentions that "the rich man also died and was buried" (v. 22b) while saying nothing about Lazarus's burial. In antiquity, denial of burial was one of the greatest imaginable indignities (cf. Sophocles' Antigone — Antigone risks death to bury her brother). That Lazarus likely received no human burial is the final earthly degradation before the divine reversal: the man no one buried is carried by angels to the seat of highest honor.

verses.text: He cried out: "Father Abraham, have mercy on me! Send Lazarus to dip just the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. I am in agony in this fire." Send Lazarus. He used the name. He had always known it.

footnotes.content: Hades (ᾅδης) is not the Greek mythological underworld, nor is it the medieval Christian "hell" of later tradition. It corresponds to the Hebrew שְׁאוֹל (Sheol) — the realm of the dead as understood in Second Temple Judaism. The divided post-mortem realm with separate sections for the righteous and wicked is attested in 1 Enoch 22, 4 Ezra, and the Apocalypse of Abraham. Jesus uses this conventional cosmographic framework as narrative furniture for his ethical argument. The parable's central claims — conscious post-mortem existence, reversal of earthly status, irreversibility — are not undermined by recognizing the parabolic character of the imagery.

The rich man uses Lazarus's name — he knew who was at his gate all along. His failure was not ignorance but willful blindness. And even in Hades, he treats Lazarus as a servant: "Send Lazarus to serve me." The condescension persists beyond death. He cannot see Lazarus as an equal even when the entire cosmic order has been reversed.

footnotes.keyword: I am in agony in this fire
footnotes.content: The image of a finger-dip of water to cool a tongue in flame is deliberately impossible as literal physical description — fingers, water, and tongues are not features of a non-physical afterlife. Three frames: (1) The literary reader recognizes parabolic imagery: these are narrative images conveying a spiritual reality (consciousness, suffering, reversal, separation), not a geography of the afterlife. (2) The existential reader finds in the torment a description of the anguish of permanent regret — to see what you refused to see, when you can no longer act. (3) The theological reader affirms conscious post-mortem existence and the seriousness of earthly moral choices without requiring the imagery to be cartographic. The parable's force does not depend on whether Hades has literal fire; it depends on whether what you do with Lazarus at your gate has consequences that outlast your lifetime.

verses.text: Abraham said:
And between us and you, a vast chasm stands fixed. No one can cross from here to you. No one can cross from there to us."

footnotes.content: Abraham addresses the rich man as τέκνον ("child") — acknowledging the kinship bond. He does not deny the covenant relationship. But the acknowledgment makes the refusal more devastating, not less. The verb ἀπέλαβες ("you received in full, you received what was owed you") is accounting language: as if the rich man's earthly luxury was an advance payment of his full eschatological portion. The eschatological reversal is not arbitrary punishment but rectification — the Torah obligated the rich to care for the poor (Deut 15; Lev 19; Isa 58), and the accounting has come due.

The perfect passive ἐστήρικται ("has been firmly fixed, stands established") is the parable's most theologically weighty verb form. It indicates a state already accomplished and permanent — the chasm was not being fixed in that moment but had already been fixed before the rich man arrived. This is eschatological finality. The impossibility of crossing operates in both directions: neither compassion from Abraham's side nor desperate effort from the rich man's can bridge it. Whatever this chasm represents — whether a metaphor for the irreversibility of moral choices or a claim about the structure of post-mortem existence — its permanence is non-negotiable in the narrative.

verses.text: I have five brothers. Let him warn them, so they don't end up here."
"They have Moses and the Prophets. Let them listen."

footnotes.content: "Moses and the Prophets" is the standard Jewish summary of the Hebrew Bible — Torah (the five books of Moses) and Nevi'im (the Prophets). Abraham's appeal to their sufficiency affirms that the Torah and the prophetic tradition already contain everything needed to know how to treat the poor: Deuteronomy 15:7–11 (open your hand to your poor brother), Leviticus 19:9–10 (leave gleanings for the poor and the foreigner), Amos 2:6–7 (judgment for selling the poor for sandals), Isaiah 58:6–7 (feeding the hungry as true fasting). The rich man did not need new revelation. He needed to read what he already had.

verses.text: "No, Father Abraham — but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent."
"If they will not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded — not even if someone rises from the dead."

footnotes.keyword: not even if someone rises from the dead
footnotes.content: The parable's final line is proleptic — it anticipates the resurrection of Jesus himself. Ancient post-resurrection listeners would have caught the irony immediately: someone DID rise from the dead, and many were still not persuaded. The shift from "goes to them from the dead" (πορευθῇ, v. 30 — the rich man's proposal) to "rises from the dead" (ἀναστῇ, v. 31 — Abraham's restatement) is significant: ἀνίστημι is the standard resurrection verb in Luke-Acts. The parable breaks its own narrative frame to address Jesus' audience directly: the problem is not insufficient evidence. It never was.

The parable's most uncomfortable claim is not about the afterlife but about the present: the evidence is already sufficient. Moses and the Prophets — the Scriptures — already command justice for the poor. No miracle, no visitation from beyond, no supernatural intervention can substitute for the willingness to see the Lazarus at your own gate. Bryan Stevenson's observation in "Just Mercy" echoes this: proximity to suffering changes people, but only if they allow themselves to see. The rich man's failure was not that he lacked information. It was that he lacked sight.

The Rich Man and Lazarus draws on a narrative framework with rabbinic parallels — a well-known story-type about rich and poor men whose fates reverse after death. Jesus' version inverts the expected logic: in the rabbinic parallel (cited by Keener), the rich man had done one good deed that secured his place, while the poor scholar had a single sin that excluded him. Jesus flips this completely — the rich man's only recorded failure is the omission of care for Lazarus at his gate, and this omission alone suffices for his condemnation. The parable's use of conventional Second Temple afterlife cosmography (1 Enoch 22; Apocalypse of Abraham) as "narrative furniture" for an ethical argument is consistent with how first-century Jewish teachers used such imagery — not as systematic eschatology but as moral illustration with eschatological stakes.
